Let \(v(n)\) be the parity vector of the prime exponents of \(n\). The zero-vector elements are \(\{1,4,9\}\). The ten distinct nonzero vectors are
\[
a,b,c,d,e,f,a+b,a+c,a+d,b+c,
\]
where \(a,b,c,d,e,f\) correspond to primes \(2,3,5,7,11,13\). The vectors \(a\) and \(b\) occur twice: \(a=\{2,8\}\), \(b=\{3,12\}\).

The forbidden nonzero triples are
\[
\{a,b,a+b\},\{a,c,a+c\},\{a,d,a+d\},\{b,c,b+c\},\{a+b,a+c,b+c\}.
\]
No single vector meets all five, so at most \(10-2=8\) distinct nonzero vector classes can be chosen if we avoid these triples.

If we choose a zero-vector element, we can choose at most two of \(\{1,4,9\}\), and no nonzero vector may be repeated. Hence
\[
|A|\le 2+8=10.
\]
If we choose no zero-vector element, a subset of size \(11\) or \(12\) is impossible: size \(12\) contains \(\{2,3,6\}\), and size \(11\) would have to omit \(6\) to break \(\{2,3,6\}\), but then \(\{2,5,10\}\) remains. Thus \(|A|\le 10\).

A valid subset of size \(10\) is
\[
\{1,4,3,5,6,7,10,11,13,14\}.
\]
So the largest possible size is \(\boxed{10}\).
